newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's Stoyanov seeks closer European links.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's Stoyanov seeks closer European links.

text.p: Bulgarian opposition candidate Petar Stoyanov claimed a decisive victory over his ex-communist rival in Sunday's presidential election and pledged to bring his country closer to the European Union and NATO.

But he was careful to avoid direct criticism of the ruling Socialists and proposed a National Salvation Council of experts and respected public figures to advise the government on how to fight deepening social and economic crisis.
"Political independence and economic stability come through integration into the European Union and the Atlantic Alliance," Stoyanov told a news conference.

Stefan Savov, leader of a small party allied to Stoyanov's Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), said Stoyanov's projected 20-point lead was a defeat not only for his Socialist presidential rival Ivan Marazov but for the government of Prime Minister Zhan Videnov.
"Our landslide victory means not only Marazov is finished but Videnov is done for too," said Savov, co-chairman of the UDF-allied People's Union.

Projections by independent polling agencies showed Stoyanov with about 59 percent of the vote against about 41 for Culture Minister Marazov. Turnout was about 60 percent, slightly below last Sunday's first round 63 percent.
Preliminary official results are expected early on Monday with the full outcome due by Wednesday.
Even workers in the smokestack industries of Bulgaria's red heartland said they had deserted the Socialists, who won a majority in parliamentary elections in December 1994.

Seven years after overthrowing their communist rulers, Bulgarians are still waiting for the benefits promised from democracy and a market economy and now face a winter of food and fuel shortages harking back to communist rule.
Bombings and other violence have marred Bulgaria's second post-communist presidential campaign, culminating in the murder last month of former prime minister Andrei Lukanov.

Shortly after Sunday's voting began, a caller telephoned a bomb threat to a city centre school where President Zhelyu Zhelev was due to cast his ballot. A thorough search found nothing, state radio said.
Zhelev, a pro-market liberal like Stoyanov, lost a U.S.-style primary in June and has not stood for re-election.
The run-off coincides with an International Monetary Fund mission discussing terms for release of a delayed $115 million credit vital to stop Bulgaria defaulting on its foreign debt.

Mission leader Anne McGuirk, who arrived on Friday, met Videnov on Sunday but made no comment. Officials described the talks as a preliminary meeting and said it was too early to expect concrete results.
Stoyanov and his UDF accuse the government of moving too slowly to privatise state firms and close big loss-makers.
Bulgaria has managed to privatise a mere five percent of state industry, with most of the cash going into the pockets of shadowy business groupings close to the Socialists.

Neighbouring Romania and Yugoslavia, also voting on Sunday, are themselves battling economic crisis but Bulgaria has the lowest foreign investment in the region and a quarter of its numerous banks are in receivership.
